I / Reading Guide

How this document slots into every context packet

This document exists to answer the question every engineer asks when they pick up a story: why this algorithm, and exactly how is it supposed to work? The persona specs describe what the UI looks like. The tech architecture describes the data models and API routes. This document describes the computational and theoretical machinery underneath — with enough precision that an implementation can be verified against the specification, not just guessed from intuition.

The scholarly-features mapping principle

Every academic claim in this document is followed immediately by its implementation consequence. "Corbett and Anderson (1995) showed BKT converges in 3–5 answers" is not useful to an engineer. "BKT converges in 3–5 answers, therefore the study queue must wait for at least 3 responses before updating clinical tier ordering" is. Every scholarly foundation in this document is written as: claim → implementation rule → where it appears in the codebase.

How to use this document in context packets

When writing a context packet for a story that touches any of the systems below, copy the relevant Algorithm Spec or DS Spec into the SCHOLARLY + DS&A CONTEXT section. Include: the algorithm name, the exact parameters used, the complexity guarantee, and the specific scholarly reference. The engineer should never need to re-derive or look up these specifications — they should be in the packet.

Context packet — SCHOLARLY + DS&A CONTEXT section (new required field)

II / Mastery Science — BKT, IRT, Pimsleur

The adaptive learning foundations — with exact implementation parameters

Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT)

Foundation · Corbett & Anderson, 1995
BKT models student knowledge as a latent binary state (known / not-known) and updates it using Bayesian inference after each response.
Implementation rule: run BKT update after every question response in study queue and practice mode. Not during exam delivery (exams are assessment, not learning). Update Supabase concept_mastery.p_mastery atomically after each response via RPC.
Corbett, A.T. & Anderson, J.R. (1995). Knowledge Tracing: Modeling the Acquisition of Procedural Knowledge. User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction, 4(4), 253–278.
Foundation · Van De Sande, 2013
BKT parameters (p_init, p_transit, p_slip, p_guess) must be constrained: p_guess + p_slip < 1, and p_slip < 0.1 to prevent the model inverting (high mastery predicted despite frequent errors).
Implementation rule: validate all four parameters at initialization. If any constraint is violated, throw at startup, not at runtime. The specific values in Journey OS (p_guess=0.20, p_slip=0.10) satisfy the constraint.
Van De Sande, B. (2013). Properties of the Bayesian Knowledge Estimation Algorithm. Proceedings of EDM 2013.
BKT Update — Full Specification
Used by: study queue, practice mode · Updated after: every response except exam
O(1) timeO(1) spaceDeterministic
// Parameters — hardcoded, not user-configurable
const BKT_PARAMS = {
  p_init:     0.10,  // prior: P(student knows concept before any exposure)
  p_transit:  0.20,  // learning: P(transitions from !know → know after one attempt)
  p_slip:     0.10,  // slip:   P(answers wrong | knows concept)
  p_guess:    0.20,  // guess:  P(answers right | does NOT know concept)
  mastery_threshold: 0.95,
}

// Update P(knows) after observing a response
function bkt_update(p_prior: number, correct: boolean): number {
  const { p_slip, p_guess, p_transit } = BKT_PARAMS

  // Step 1: posterior given observation (Bayes update)
  let p_posterior: number
  if (correct) {
    // P(knows | correct) = P(knows)*P(correct|knows) / P(correct)
    const p_correct_knows   = 1 - p_slip
    const p_correct_unknown = p_guess
    p_posterior = (p_prior * p_correct_knows)
                / (p_prior * p_correct_knows + (1 - p_prior) * p_correct_unknown)
  } else {
    // P(knows | wrong)   = P(knows)*P(wrong|knows) / P(wrong)
    const p_wrong_knows   = p_slip
    const p_wrong_unknown = 1 - p_guess
    p_posterior = (p_prior * p_wrong_knows)
                / (p_prior * p_wrong_knows + (1 - p_prior) * p_wrong_unknown)
  }

  // Step 2: apply learning (P of transitioning from !know → know)
  const p_next = p_posterior + (1 - p_posterior) * p_transit

  // Step 3: clamp to [0.001, 0.999] — never allow absolute certainty
  return Math.max(0.001, Math.min(0.999, p_next))
}

// Mastery test
const is_mastered = (p: number) => p >= BKT_PARAMS.mastery_threshold
Invariant: p_mastery ∈ (0,1) always Invariant: concept exits daily queue iff p_mastery ≥ 0.95 Warning: do NOT run BKT during exam delivery — pollutes mastery before scoring

Pimsleur Decay — Spaced Repetition Schedule

Foundation · Pimsleur, 1967 + Ebbinghaus, 1885
Recall probability decays exponentially with time since last review. Optimal review intervals follow a geometric progression (approximately doubling each time) for retention with minimum review sessions.
Implementation rule: each time a concept achieves mastery (p_mastery ≥ 0.95), schedule the NEXT review at review_intervals[current_review_count] days in the future. Store next_review_at as a timestamp on concept_mastery. The BKT model continues to apply at every review — a wrong answer at a late review will drop p_mastery sharply.
Pimsleur, P. (1967). A Memory Schedule. Modern Language Journal, 51(2), 73–75. · Ebbinghaus, H. (1885/1913). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology.
Pimsleur Decay Scheduler
Used by: study queue scheduling · After every mastery event and every correct response at a scheduled review
O(1) timeDeterministic
// Review intervals in days: geometric progression (Pimsleur-modified)
const REVIEW_INTERVALS = [1, 3, 7, 14, 30, 60, 120, Infinity]

// schedule_next_review: called after BKT update when correct
function schedule_next_review(
  review_count: number,  // how many times reviewed at this interval tier
  p_mastery: number
): Date | null {
  if (p_mastery < BKT_PARAMS.mastery_threshold) {
    return new Date()  // not mastered → back in today's queue immediately
  }

  const interval_days = REVIEW_INTERVALS[Math.min(review_count, REVIEW_INTERVALS.length - 1)]
  if (interval_days === Infinity) return null  // fully consolidated — exits queue

  const next = new Date()
  next.setDate(next.getDate() + interval_days)
  return next
}

// compute current p_mastery after decay
function apply_decay(p_last: number, days_elapsed: number): number {
  // λ is concept-specific; default decay constant = 0.05 per day
  const DECAY_CONSTANT = 0.05
  return p_last * Math.exp(-DECAY_CONSTANT * days_elapsed)
}
Invariant: no concept can sit in queue with next_review_at > 7 days without a mastery event Clinical-tier override: Tier 1 concepts decay 2× faster (DECAY_CONSTANT = 0.10)

Item Response Theory (IRT 3PL) — Practice Mode Selection

Foundation · Birnbaum, 1968 · Lord, 1980
The three-parameter logistic model (3PL-IRT) captures item discrimination (a), difficulty (b), and guessing (c) in a single probability function. The Fisher information function I(θ) identifies which item, at a given student ability θ, provides maximum information — i.e., narrows ability estimation most.
Implementation rule: during adaptive practice, estimate current theta (θ) from recent response history using EAP (Expected A Posteriori). Select the item from the available pool with difficulty parameter b closest to θ, weighted by discrimination a. Never show the same item twice in a session (exclude by item_id set).
Birnbaum, A. (1968). Some latent trait models and their use in inferring an examinee's ability. In Lord & Novick, Statistical Theories of Mental Test Scores. · Lord, F.M. (1980). Applications of IRT to Practical Testing Problems. Lawrence Erlbaum.
IRT 3PL — Probability + Fisher Information + EAP Theta Estimation
Used by: practice mode item selection · theta updated after each practice response
O(n) item selectO(k) EAPAdaptive
// 3PL Item Response Function
// θ: student ability (-3 to +3); a: discrimination (0.5–2.5); b: difficulty; c: guessing (0.0–0.35)
function p3pl(theta: number, a: number, b: number, c: number): number {
  return c + (1 - c) / (1 + Math.exp(-1.7 * a * (theta - b)))
}

// Fisher Information at ability θ for a given item
// Higher information = item is more useful at this ability level
function fisher_info(theta: number, a: number, b: number, c: number): number {
  const p = p3pl(theta, a, b, c)
  const q = 1 - p
  // Avoid division by zero and near-zero probabilities
  if (p < 0.001 || q < 0.001) return 0
  return ((1.7 * a) ** 2) * ((p - c) ** 2) * q / ((1 - c) ** 2 * p)
}

// EAP Theta Estimation: numerical integration over quadrature points
// X_i: quadrature points (-4 to +4 in 41 steps)
// W_i: normal prior weights N(0,1) at each point
function eap_theta(responses: {correct: boolean, a:number, b:number, c:number}[]): number {
  const QUADRATURE = Array.from({length: 41}, (_, i) => ({
    x: -4 + i * 0.2,
    w: normalPDF(0, 1, -4 + i * 0.2)
  }))

  let numerator = 0, denominator = 0
  for (const { x, w } of QUADRATURE) {
    // Likelihood of all responses at ability x
    const L = responses.reduce((acc, r) => {
      const p = p3pl(x, r.a, r.b, r.c)
      return acc * (r.correct ? p : 1 - p)
    }, 1)
    numerator   += x * L * w
    denominator += L * w
  }
  return denominator > 0 ? numerator / denominator : 0
}

// Select best item for current theta from available pool
function select_item(theta: number, items: Item[], used: Set<string>): Item {
  return items
    .filter(item => !used.has(item.id))
    .sort((a, b) => fisher_info(theta, b.irt_a, b.irt_b, b.irt_c)
                  - fisher_info(theta, a.irt_a, a.irt_b, a.irt_c))
  [0]
}
Default item params when IRT not calibrated: a=1.0, b=0.0, c=0.20 IRT calibration: requires ≥30 student responses per item before reliable a/b/c estimation Theta bounds: clamp to [-4, +4] in all operations
III / Assessment Science — ECD, Psychometrics, Standard Setting

The validity chain from evidence to score — every claim defended

Evidence-Centered Design (ECD)

Foundation · Mislevy, Steinberg & Almond, 2003
Valid assessment requires a chain: Student Model (what we claim to know about the student) → Evidence Model (what observations we use as evidence) → Task Model (what tasks elicit the evidence). An item without an explicit evidence model cannot be used to make valid inferences about student ability.
Implementation rule: every generated item must include a Toulmin validation chain stored in assessment_items.toulmin_chain (JSONB). The chain has four fields: claim (what ability is being tested), warrant (why this item tests that ability), evidence_grade (A/B/C/D based on source quality), and backing (the curriculum/UMLS basis). Items with null toulmin_chain are blocked from exam use by RLS policy.
Mislevy, R.J., Steinberg, L.S., & Almond, R.G. (2003). On the structure of educational assessments. Measurement, 1(1), 3–62.
Foundation · Haladyna, Downing & Rodriguez, 2002
NBME-style multiple-choice items must: (1) use clinical vignettes for application-level items, (2) have one unambiguously correct answer, (3) have distractors grounded in plausible misconceptions (not arbitrary wrong facts), and (4) avoid clues in the stem that reveal the correct answer.
Implementation rule: the generation prompt for every item includes these four rules verbatim as a system constraint. The QA scorer checks for each of them specifically. Items that fail rules 2 or 3 are marked qa_status = 'failed' and must be regenerated, not manually edited.
Haladyna, T.M., Downing, S.M., & Rodriguez, M.C. (2002). A review of multiple-choice item-writing guidelines for classroom assessment. Applied Measurement in Education, 15(3), 309–334.

Reliability (KR-20) and Standard Setting (Angoff)

Foundation · Cronbach, 1951 (KR-20)
Kuder-Richardson Formula 20 (KR-20) measures internal consistency reliability for dichotomous items. KR-20 ≥ 0.70 is the accepted minimum for high-stakes educational assessment. Below this threshold, score-based pass/fail decisions cannot be defended.
Implementation rule: compute KR-20 after every completed exam with ≥10 students. Store in exam_analytics.kr20. If KR-20 < 0.70 on a summative exam, flag to Department Chair for review. Formula: KR-20 = (n/(n-1)) * (1 - Σ(pᵢqᵢ)/σ²) where pᵢ = proportion correct for item i, qᵢ = 1-pᵢ, σ² = variance of total scores.
Kuder, G.F. & Richardson, M.W. (1937). The theory of the estimation of test reliability. Psychometrika, 2(3), 151–160. · Criterion: Nunnally (1978). Psychometric Theory, 2nd ed.
Foundation · Angoff, 1971 (Standard Setting)
The Angoff method produces defensible cut scores by asking subject-matter experts to estimate, for each item: "What proportion of minimally competent students would answer this correctly?" The cut score is the mean of these estimates across all items and all judges.
Implementation rule: the Chair's Angoff simulation tool collects one rating per item per rater. Store ratings in angoff_ratings table. Compute cut score as MEAN(rater_means). Report inter-rater agreement (SD of rater means); if SD > 10 percentage points, prompt a consensus discussion before adopting the cut score.
Angoff, W.H. (1971). Scales, norms, and equivalent scores. In R.L. Thorndike (Ed.), Educational Measurement (2nd ed., pp. 508–600). ACE.

Differential Item Functioning (DIF) — Equity Analysis

Foundation · Holland & Thayer, 1988 (Mantel-Haenszel DIF)
An item exhibits DIF if students of equal ability but different demographic groups have different probabilities of answering correctly. DIF detection requires conditioning on total test score (as a proxy for ability) and comparing focal vs. reference group performance within score strata.
Implementation rule: compute Mantel-Haenszel chi-squared for each item after every exam with ≥50 students. ETS DIF classification: A (|MH D-DIF| < 1.0) = negligible; B (1.0–1.5) = moderate; C (>1.5) = large. Items classified B or C are flagged in the Chair's DIF table for review. Never auto-remove items — faculty review required.
Holland, P.W. & Thayer, D.T. (1988). Differential item performance and the Mantel-Haenszel procedure. In Wainer & Braun (Eds.), Test Validity (pp. 129–145). Erlbaum.
KR-20 Reliability Computation
Used by: exam analytics (post-exam) · Required for: summative exams ≥10 students
O(n·k)n=students, k=items
// responses: n×k boolean matrix (student i answered item j correctly)
function kr20(responses: boolean[][]): number {
  const n = responses.length        // number of students
  const k = responses[0].length     // number of items

  // Total scores per student
  const scores = responses.map(row => row.filter(Boolean).length)
  const mean_score = scores.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / n
  const variance   = scores.reduce((a, b) => a + (b - mean_score) ** 2, 0) / n

  // p_i = proportion correct per item, q_i = 1-p_i
  const pq_sum = Array.from({length: k}, (_, j) => {
    const p = responses.filter(row => row[j]).length / n
    return p * (1 - p)
  }).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)

  return (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - pq_sum / variance)
}

// DIF: Mantel-Haenszel chi-squared (simplified)
function mantel_haenszel_dif(
  focal_correct: number[],    // scores of focal group (URM) for this item, by total-score stratum
  focal_n: number[],
  ref_correct: number[],      // scores of reference group (non-URM), by stratum
  ref_n: number[]
): { chi2: number, mh_d_dif: number, category: 'A'|'B'|'C' } {
  // compute Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio across strata, then convert to D-DIF
  // Full implementation: see psychometrics library (R's difR package as reference)
  // MH D-DIF = -2.35 * ln(alpha_MH) where alpha_MH is the MH odds ratio
  // ETS classification: |D-DIF| < 1.0 = A, 1.0-1.5 = B, >1.5 = C
  // ...
}
IV / Knowledge Representation — UMLS, Hetionet, LOD

The scholarly basis for the three-hub knowledge graph topology

Foundation · Bodenreider, 2004 (UMLS Metathesaurus)
UMLS provides normalized Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs) that serve as a shared vocabulary across 200+ biomedical vocabularies including MeSH, SNOMED CT, ICD-10, and RxNorm. CUI-grounded concept nodes enable cross-source linking without terminology conflicts.
Implementation rule: every SubConcept node in Neo4j must carry either a umls_cui or a umls_cui_candidates array. Nodes with empty umls_cui are stored as unverified SubConcepts and cannot participate in coverage scoring until reviewed. MetaMap/QuickUMLS produces CUI candidates — faculty must confirm or adjust.
Bodenreider, O. (2004). The Unified Medical Language System (UMLS): Integrating biomedical terminology. Nucleic Acids Research, 32(Database issue), D267–D270.
Foundation · Himmelstein et al., 2017 (Hetionet)
Hetionet integrates 29 databases into a heterogeneous knowledge graph with 11 node types and 24 relationship types. Drug-disease-gene-pathway triples enable "explain why this drug treats this disease" queries not answerable from any single database.
Implementation rule: during P2 enrichment, query Hetionet for each SubConcept's CUI to extract: treats(Drug, Disease), causes(Drug, SideEffect), binds(Drug, Gene), associates(Gene, Disease). Store enriched triples as SubConcept.lod_facts JSONB array. Display in the faculty "This Week" intelligence view and in student Why Wrong? explanations when pharmacology-related.
Himmelstein, D.S. et al. (2017). Systematic integration of biomedical knowledge prioritizes drugs for repurposing. eLife, 6, e26726.
Foundation · Three-Hub Topology Design Decision (D06)
A single monolithic concept node cannot simultaneously serve as a learning unit (BKT state), a pedagogical target (SLO alignment), and an assessment anchor (USMLE mapping) without role confusion. Separating these concerns into three hubs (SubConcept → SLO → USMLE_Subtopic) allows each to evolve independently.
Implementation rule: never add USMLE_Subtopic properties to SubConcept, and never add pedagogical metadata to USMLE_Subtopic. The relationship SubConcept-[:MAPS_TO]→USMLE_Subtopic carries the mapping confidence score. SLO-[:CONTRIBUTES_TO]→ILO is always directed from course-level to institution-level.

Evidence Grade Weights — LOD Source Quality

GradeWeightSource typesExample
A1.00Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, RCTsCochrane review on heart failure mortality
B0.82Prospective cohort studies, large RCTsSOLVD trial on enalapril in HFrEF
C0.65Expert guidelines, textbooks, case seriesACC/AHA Heart Failure Guidelines 2022
D0.45Expert opinion, case reports, LOD inferenceHetionet drug-disease path without clinical trial

Evidence grade weights are used in coverage scoring: coverage_score += evidence_grade_weight / 3.0, capped at 1.0. An item backed only by Grade D evidence counts for less coverage than one backed by Grade A. This incentivizes using high-quality sources in content generation.

V / Algorithm Catalog

18 algorithms — pseudocode, complexity, security properties, and where each is used

Fisher-Yates Shuffle — Seeded (Exam Scrambling)
Used by: exam delivery (C02) · item order + option order scrambling per student
O(n)DeterministicSecurity-critical
// Seeded with HMAC-SHA256 to ensure unpredictability without secret key
function exam_scramble(
  items: Item[],
  student_id: string,
  exam_id: string
): Item[] {
  // HMAC-SHA256 produces 32 bytes of keyed pseudorandom data
  // EXAM_SCRAMBLE_SECRET is a 32-byte env var, never logged or exposed
  const seed_bytes = hmac_sha256(
    process.env.EXAM_SCRAMBLE_SECRET!,
    `${student_id}:${exam_id}`
  )

  // Expand seed into a deterministic PRNG (xorshift64)
  const rng = xorshift64(seed_bytes.readBigUInt64LE(0))

  // Fisher-Yates in-place shuffle (Knuth 2011 vol. 2)
  const arr = [...items]
  for (let i = arr.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
    const j = Number(rng.next() % BigInt(i + 1))
    ;[arr[i], arr[j]] = [arr[j], arr[i]]
  }

  // Scramble options for each item using a derived seed
  arr.forEach((item, idx) => {
    const opt_seed = xorshift64(seed_bytes.readBigUInt64LE(8) ^ BigInt(idx))
    item.options = fisher_yates(item.options, opt_seed)
  })

  return arr
}

Security property: Without the EXAM_SCRAMBLE_SECRET, a student cannot pre-compute their item order even if they know their student_id and exam_id. The scramble is deterministic — a student who reconnects mid-exam sees the same order. Two students with different student_ids see different orders (with overwhelming probability from HMAC collision resistance).

EXAM_SCRAMBLE_SECRET must be 32+ bytes, stored in Supabase Vault, never in .env.local Idempotent: same student_id + exam_id always produces same shuffle
Priority Queue Study Scheduler — Min-Heap
Used by: study queue daily compilation · runs nightly via Inngest scheduled job
O(n log n) buildO(log n) updateDeterministic
// Priority key: tuple compared lexicographically
// Lower key = higher priority (min-heap)
type QueueKey = [
  clinical_tier: number,  // 1=immediately life-threatening, 4=benign (lower=higher priority)
  neg_mastery: number,   // -p_mastery (lower=higher priority = weaker mastery)
  review_due_ms: number, // Date.now() of next_review_at (earlier due = higher priority)
  concept_id: string,   // tiebreaker — deterministic ordering
]

function build_daily_queue(
  student_id: string,
  goal_count: number,    // from student settings: 5/12/20
  today: Date
): ConceptId[] {
  // Fetch all due concepts from Supabase (next_review_at <= today)
  const due = fetch_due_concepts(student_id, today)

  // Build min-heap on QueueKey
  const heap = new MinHeap<QueueKey>()
  for (const c of due) {
    heap.push([
      c.clinical_tier,
      -c.p_mastery,
      c.next_review_at.getTime(),
      c.concept_id
    ], c.concept_id)
  }

  // Extract top goal_count items
  const queue: string[] = []
  while (queue.length < goal_count && !heap.isEmpty()) {
    queue.push(heap.pop())
  }
  return queue
}
Invariant: clinical Tier 1 concepts always precede Tier 4 concepts at the same p_mastery level Invariant: new concepts (p_mastery = p_init = 0.10) appear before decaying mastered concepts
Hash Chain — FERPA Audit Log Tamper Detection
Used by: FERPA audit log (trigger-written) · integrity verification by admin
O(1) insertO(n) verifySecurity-critical
-- Postgres trigger (runs at INSERT on ferpa_audit_log, BEFORE write)
-- Using pgcrypto SHA-256
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ferpa_audit_chain_hash() RETURNS trigger AS $$
DECLARE
  prev_hash TEXT;
BEGIN
  -- Get the hash of the previous row (or genesis sentinel for first row)
  SELECT chain_hash INTO prev_hash
    FROM ferpa_audit_log
    ORDER BY created_at DESC
    LIMIT 1;

  IF prev_hash IS NULL THEN
    prev_hash := encode(digest('GENESIS:' || NEW.institution_id, 'sha256'), 'hex');
  END IF;

  -- Hash = SHA256(previous_hash || this_row_id || event_type || student_id || timestamp)
  NEW.chain_hash := encode(digest(
    prev_hash ||
    NEW.id::text ||
    NEW.event_type ||
    NEW.student_id ||
    extract(epoch from NEW.created_at)::text,
    'sha256'
  ), 'hex');

  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql SECURITY DEFINER;

Tamper detection: If any row in the log is modified or deleted, all subsequent chain hashes become invalid. Verification walks the chain linearly and fails on the first mismatch, pinpointing exactly which row was altered. The chain is written by a SECURITY DEFINER function — application code cannot override it.

NEVER grant UPDATE or DELETE on ferpa_audit_log to any role, including service_role Verification endpoint: admin-only, read-only, logs its own access to the chain
Token Bucket — Generation Rate Limiting
Used by: P3 generation pipeline · per-faculty daily and concurrent limits (C10)
O(1)Smooth burst-tolerant
// Token bucket per faculty_id in Redis (via Upstash)
// Max daily budget: 100 items/day (configurable per faculty by admin)
// Max burst: 20 items in a single request
// Refill rate: max_daily_items / 86400 items/second = 0.00116 items/sec

async function check_generation_limit(
  faculty_id: string,
  requested_items: number
): Promise<{ allowed: boolean, tokens_remaining: number }> {
  const key = `gen_limit:${faculty_id}`
  const max_daily = await get_faculty_limit(faculty_id)  // from Supabase admin config
  const refill_rate = max_daily / (24 * 60 * 60)            // tokens per second
  const max_burst = Math.min(requested_items, 20)

  // Atomic Redis operation: read current tokens + last_refill, compute new tokens
  const [tokens, last_refill] = await redis.hmget(key, 'tokens', 'last_refill')
  const now = Date.now() / 1000
  const elapsed = now - (parseFloat(last_refill) || now)
  const new_tokens = Math.min(max_daily, parseFloat(tokens || '0') + elapsed * refill_rate)

  if (new_tokens >= requested_items) {
    await redis.hmset(key, {tokens: new_tokens - requested_items, last_refill: now})
    return { allowed: true, tokens_remaining: new_tokens - requested_items }
  }
  return { allowed: false, tokens_remaining: new_tokens }
}
Inngest concurrency key: journey/items.batch-generate → concurrencyKey: faculty/${id}, limit: 3 Institution-level cost cap: separate monthly budget in generation_limits table — checked before Redis
Coverage Bit Vector — O(1) USMLE Coverage Query
Used by: USMLE readiness tracker, advisor at-risk detection, dean equity dashboard
O(1) set/getO(n/64) countMemory-efficient
// Step 1 taxonomy: 987 topics → bit vector of 124 bytes (ceil(987/8))
// Step 2 taxonomy: 1,462 topics → 183 bytes
// Stored as: bytea in Supabase (usmle_coverage.step1_bits)

class CoverageBits {
  private bits: Uint8Array

  constructor(topic_count: number) {
    this.bits = new Uint8Array(Math.ceil(topic_count / 8))
  }

  // Mark a topic as covered — O(1)
  set(topic_id: number): void {
    this.bits[topic_id >> 3] |= (1 << (topic_id & 7))
  }

  // Check if a topic is covered — O(1)
  get(topic_id: number): boolean {
    return Boolean((this.bits[topic_id >> 3] >> (topic_id & 7)) & 1)
  }

  // Count covered topics — O(n/8) using popcount
  count(): number {
    let n = 0
    for (const byte of this.bits) {
      // Brian Kernighan's popcount — O(set bits per byte)
      let b = byte
      while (b) { n++; b &= b - 1 }
    }
    return n
  }

  // Union (merge coverage from multiple exams/sessions) — O(n/8)
  union(other: CoverageBits): CoverageBits {
    const result = new CoverageBits(this.bits.length * 8)
    for (let i = 0; i < this.bits.length; i++) {
      result.bits[i] = this.bits[i] | other.bits[i]
    }
    return result
  }
}
Memory: 124 bytes per student for Step 1 · vs 987 rows in a join table Update trigger: append to bit vector on every exam_attempt INSERT that maps items → USMLE topics
VI / Data Structure Catalog

12 data structures — chosen for Journey OS's exact access patterns

Min-Heap (Study Queue)
insert O(log n)pop O(log n)
Why not array?
O(n) to find minimum vs O(log n) with heap. Study queue has 100–5,000 due concepts per student.
Key structure
(clinical_tier, -p_mastery, review_due_ms, concept_id) — tuple comparison, lexicographic
Where
Built nightly in Inngest scheduled job. Serialized as JSONB array to Supabase student_queues.
HNSW Index (Vector Search)
query O(log n)insert O(log n)
Config
m=16, ef_construction=200, ef_search=50 — balances recall vs. latency
Why HNSW over IVFFlat?
HNSW has no training phase and handles incremental inserts (new chunks added per lecture). IVFFlat requires periodic re-indexing.
Where
pgvector index on chunks.embedding (1536-dim). Used for HyDE search, similar item detection.
Bloom Filter (Item Deduplication)
O(k) checkNo false negatives
Parameters
m=10,000 bits · k=7 hash functions · n≤1000 items → FP rate ≈ 0.8%
Use case
Before generating new items for a SubConcept, check if ≥3 approved items already exist. Bloom filter provides fast "definitely no items" check before DB query.
Scoped by
One Bloom filter per faculty_id × subconcept_id pair. Stored in Redis, expires after 24h.
Sparse Mastery Matrix (BKT State)
O(1) avg lookupMemory-efficient
Problem
Full matrix: 312 students × 12,000 SubConcepts = 3.7M rows. Most cells empty (students haven't seen most concepts).
Solution
Sparse: only rows where student has seen concept. Hash map in application; B-tree index on (student_id, concept_id) in Postgres.
Row structure
concept_mastery: {student_id, concept_id, p_mastery, review_count, next_review_at, last_updated}
Coverage Bit Vector (USMLE Readiness)
O(1) set/getO(n/64) count
Size
Step 1: 124 bytes. Step 2: 183 bytes. Per student. vs. ~7.9KB for a boolean array.
Operations
OR-union across sessions (bitwise), popcount for coverage %, gap detection via AND-NOT against full taxonomy
Storage
bytea in Postgres. Read into Uint8Array in TypeScript for manipulation.
Hash Chain (FERPA Audit Log)
O(1) insertTamper-evident
Structure
Linked list of SHA-256 hashes. Each node's hash includes the previous node's hash.
Property
Modifying any entry invalidates all subsequent hashes — detectable by linear scan.
Verification cost
O(n) full chain re-hash. Typically only verified on audit request, not on every read.

VII / Security Primitives

Six security-critical patterns — each with invariants that must survive every PR

Security invariants are non-negotiable

The invariants listed in this section must be verifiable by a CI check. Each one corresponds to a test in tests/shared/security.spec.ts. If any invariant is broken by a PR, the CI must fail. Engineers should treat these the same as compilation errors — not optional, not "we'll fix it later."

RLS policy specification — critical tables

-- concept_mastery: students see only their own rows
CREATE POLICY "student sees own mastery" ON concept_mastery
  FOR SELECT USING (student_id = auth.uid());

-- exam_attempts: student sees own; faculty sees own course; advisor sees advisee
CREATE POLICY "exam attempt access" ON exam_attempts
  FOR SELECT USING (
    student_id = auth.uid()                              -- own attempt
    OR institution_id IN (                               -- faculty: course-level only
      SELECT institution_id FROM faculty WHERE user_id = auth.uid()
    )
    OR student_id IN (                                   -- advisor: advisee only
      SELECT student_id FROM advisor_assignments WHERE advisor_id = auth.uid()
    )
  );

-- ferpa_audit_log: SELECT only for admin role; NO INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE via RLS
-- (writes are trigger-only, via SECURITY DEFINER function)
CREATE POLICY "ferpa admin read only" ON ferpa_audit_log
  FOR SELECT USING (
    EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM admin_users WHERE user_id = auth.uid())
  );

At-risk gap type classifier — algorithm specification

At-Risk Gap Type Classifier — Isolated / Cluster / Systemic
Used by: advisor dashboard · nightly job, result cached for 24h
O(V+E) graph scanDeterministic
// Input: student's concept_mastery array for all seen concepts
// Output: { type: 'isolated'|'cluster'|'systemic', affected_systems: string[], roots: ConceptId[] }

function classify_risk_gap(mastery: ConceptMastery[]): GapClassification {
  const weak = mastery.filter(m => m.p_mastery < 0.70)
  const weak_systems = new Set(weak.map(m => m.usmle_system))

  // Rule 1: SYSTEMIC — weakness spans ≥3 unrelated USMLE systems
  // "Unrelated" = not anatomically adjacent (Cardio + Pulmo are adjacent; Cardio + Neurology are not)
  const unrelated_systems = count_unrelated_systems(weak_systems)
  if (unrelated_systems >= 3) {
    return { type: 'systemic', affected_systems: [...weak_systems], roots: [] }
  }

  // Rule 2: CLUSTER — weak concepts are causally linked (Neo4j path exists between them)
  // Run BFS from each weak concept; if ≥2 weak concepts are reachable from a common ancestor
  // that is also weak or borderline → cluster
  const cluster_root = find_cluster_root(weak.map(m => m.concept_id))
  if (cluster_root) {
    return { type: 'cluster', affected_systems: [...weak_systems], roots: [cluster_root] }
  }

  // Rule 3: ISOLATED — one concept or a few unconnected concepts below threshold
  return { type: 'isolated', affected_systems: [...weak_systems], roots: weak.map(m => m.concept_id) }
}

// find_cluster_root: BFS on Neo4j prerequisite graph
// Returns concept_id of the "root cause" — the upstream concept whose weakness explains all others
async function find_cluster_root(weak_ids: string[]): Promise<string|null> {
  const cypher = `
    MATCH (root:SubConcept)-[:PREREQUISITE_FOR*1..3]->(weak:SubConcept)
    WHERE weak.concept_id IN $weak_ids
    AND root.concept_id IN $weak_ids
    RETURN root.concept_id, count(*) AS downstream_count
    ORDER BY downstream_count DESC LIMIT 1
  `
  return await neo4jQuery(cypher, { weak_ids }, ctx)
}
Systemic threshold: ≥3 unrelated systems · Cluster threshold: ≥2 concepts with shared prerequisite Result cached 24h in advisor_risk_cache table — stale OK, recalculated nightly
